content: The occurrence and underlying causes of injuries related to physical activities, such as walking, running, and sports, particularly in individuals aged 10 to 13, are not well understood. During the early stages of research in this area, scientists were only beginning to investigate the epidemiology and risk factors associated with exercise-related injuries. Currently, the risk factors for injuries in physically active men remain poorly defined, and the specific risks for women who engage in exercise are even less comprehensively understood. Among civilian populations, studies on runners have provided the most detailed insights into injury incidence and some associated risk factors. In contrast, research on military populations offers sex-specific data on injury risks linked to physical training and exercise. These studies benefit from controlled activities and access to complete and detailed health records, physical examinations, and fitness assessments. Research on basic combat training, which is conducted across all branches of the military and involves activities such as running, marching, and other weight-bearing aerobic exercises, often yields findings that are relevant to civilian populations. The uniformity of training within military units provides a unique opportunity to control for the variability typically observed in exercise routines among civilians. Factors such as age, sex, prior injuries, health behaviors, sports participation, physical fitness, and anatomical characteristics are considered in these studies. This report, published in the March 31, 2000, issue of the MMWR, examines both civilian and military research related to weight-bearing aerobic exercises and associated injuries. Activities such as running, walking, and aerobic dance are highlighted due to their popularity and frequent prescription as forms of exercise. Military studies on training-related injuries are presented to identify shared and sex-specific intrinsic risk factors. While risks for men are discussed briefly for comparative purposes, the primary focus of this report is on modifiable risk factors, which form the basis for recommendations on injury prevention and future research. In this report, distinctions between the terms physical activity, exercise, and physical training are emphasized. Physical activity is defined as movement produced by skeletal muscle contractions that result in energy expenditure. Exercise is a subset of physical activity that is planned, repetitive, and designed to improve or maintain at least one health-related component of physical fitness. Physical training, as used in the military, refers to organized exercise aimed at enhancing fitness. The terms exercise and physical training are used interchangeably in this context. Physical fitness is categorized into five health-related components: a) cardiorespiratory endurance (aerobic fitness), b) muscle endurance, c) strength, d) flexibility, and e) body composition. The focus of this report is on exercise for women, specifically targeting the enhancement of cardiorespiratory endurance (aerobic fitness). Unless otherwise stated, statistical significance is set at a p-value of 0.05.
